subject: regcf
note: Interpretive forks in the COMMITTED corpus (regcf.l4). Distinct from jl4/examples/legal/regcf/denovo/fork-register.json, which registers 26 forks found by the independent de novo encoding of the same Part and describes a different file — do not merge the two without re-deriving each entry against the file it names. Every entry here was already argued in prose before it was registered: F-501A-ENDPOINT and F-4A6B-MEASURE in README.md §5 and §3, F-501A-LEAPDAY in README.md §5.2 as of 2026-08-05. Registering them changes nothing about the encoding; it moves the disclosure from prose a drafter chose to write into structure the explainer renders whether or not anyone remembers. Three more (F-501A4-NEXUS, F-501A4-DETERMINER, F-501A4-SIMILAR) were added 2026-08-09 when Rule 501(a)(4) stopped being one ~300-character boolean and became six fields; all three were forced by the split and none of them could have been asked while the limb was one self-assessed fact. COMPLETENESS IS UNFALSIFIABLE: no procedure enumerates the ambiguities a statute contains, so seven entries here is not a claim that there are seven.

source.quote: during the one-year period beginning when the securities were issued

readings.description: One year after 29 February 2024 is 28 February 2025 — the anniversary clamps back to the last day of the corresponding month when the original day does not exist in it.
One year after 29 February 2024 is 1 March 2025 — the period runs a full year and lands on the next day that exists, so the restriction is one day longer.

taken.rationale: Taken because it is what the target systems already do, so the L4 answer and every exported answer agree by construction rather than by care. MEASURED 2026-08-05: `daydate`'s `add years` clamps, Excel's EDATE clamps, and FEEL's `date + duration("P1Y")` returns 2025-02-28 on both Drools/KIE 8.44.0.Final and Camunda 8.7.6. The rejected reading is not wrong as law — a court could plainly hold that a one-year period from 29 February ends on 1 March — it is simply not the reading any engine implements, and an encoding that took it would answer differently from its own DMN export. Note the third possibility that is NOT a reading of the law but a defect: reconstructing the date as `date(y + 1, m, d)` yields null on both engines, because 29 February 2025 is not a date at all.

witnesses: A transfer of securities issued 2024-02-29 and transferred 2025-02-28 is OUTSIDE the restricted period under `clamp` and INSIDE it under `rollForward`. One day, one holding in roughly four.
notes: This fork became visible only when the encoding stopped carrying an elapsed day count and started carrying dates. While `Transfer` held `days since the securities were issued`, the question could not be asked in the corpus's own vocabulary.

site.anchor: `transfer is within the one-year restricted period`

source.quote: during the one-year period beginning when the securities were issued

readings.description: The first anniversary is OUTSIDE the period: a transfer on the anniversary itself is free. The interval is [issuance, first anniversary).
The first anniversary is INSIDE the period: a transfer on the anniversary is still restricted, and freedom begins the following day.

taken.rationale: Taken as the ordinary reading of a period that BEGINS on a date: the period contains its start and not its end, as a one-year lease from 1 June ends before 1 June. The rule does not decide it, and NO ENCODING CAN — this is not a gap in the formalisation but an underdetermination in the source. A drafter could remove the question in four words; a reader who cares must litigate it.

witnesses: A transfer exactly on the first anniversary is permitted under `halfOpen` and prohibited under `closed`. Asserted both ways in regcf.l4's leap-case block.
notes: Unlike F-501A-LEAPDAY, this one has no engine-convention tiebreak available: the target systems have nothing to say about which endpoint a statute means.

site.anchor: `the applicable measure of annual income or net worth`

source.quote: the greater of $2,500, or 5 percent of the greater of the investor's annual income or net worth

readings.description: The limit is computed on the GREATER of annual income and net worth — the rule as amended in 2021.
The limit is computed on the LESSER of the two — the rule as originally adopted, and what the statute's own text at 15 U.S.C. 77d(a)(6)(B) still says.

taken.rationale: Taken for rule dates from 2021-03-15 because the regulation says so, and the corpus's rule-version axis carries `lesserOf` for earlier dates rather than discarding it — so both readings are live and selected by date rather than one being deleted. What the encoding does NOT resolve is that neither reading was ever compelled: Securities Act § 4(a)(6)(B) (15 U.S.C. 77d(a)(6)(B)) says only 'a given percentage of the annual income or net worth of such investor, as applicable', specifying neither measure, and the Commission itself notes that '[t]he statutory language does not expressly provide that the investor use the lesser of annual income or net worth' (86 FR 3496, n.460). So the operative word is a discretionary regulatory gloss held for five years and then reversed — not a conflict with the statute. CORRECTED 2026-08-06: this rationale previously read 'the statute the regulation implements still reads lesser of', which is false — the phrase appears nowhere in § 77d — and regcf.l4:394-403 had it right all along. The false form was copied out of here into three pipeline documents before it was caught.

witnesses: An investor with $110,000 income and $115,000 net worth gets a different limit under each reading; both are exercised by the committed relocation cases in regcf-corpus.cases.json.
notes: This is the fork the explainer already discussed in prose before there was a register — 'the statute is ambiguous, the regulator glossed it twice, and the encoding resolves neither'. Registering it is what stops that passage from being the only place it is said.

source.quote: The aggregate amount of securities sold to all investors by the issuer in reliance on section 4(a)(6) of the Securities Act (15 U.S.C. 77d(a)(6)) during the 12-month period preceding the date of such offer or sale, including the securities offered in such transaction, shall not exceed $5,000,000

citations.cite: 15 U.S.C. 77d(a)(6)(A), which 17 CFR 227.100(a)(1) is read against ("is not more than $1,000,000")

readings.description: The offering cap is $5,000,000, as 17 CFR 227.100(a)(1) states in terms.

citations.cite: Release 33-10884 (2020), raising the cap; Part 227 Authority note claims 15 U.S.C. 77z-3

readings.description: The offering cap is $1,000,000, the figure Congress wrote into the paragraph the exemption is granted by, and which has never been amended.
readings.foreclosure: Foreclosed by the operative text, not by any argument against it. 17 CFR 227.100(a)(1) is what an issuer files against and what the Commission administers, so no filer can rely on the statutory figure and no encoding that took it would describe the law anyone is administered under. What has NOT happened is anyone refuting it: 15 U.S.C. 77d(a)(6)(A) says $1,000,000, has never been amended to say otherwise, and sits in the very paragraph the exemption is granted by. Were a court to hold that s 28 does not reach a numeric cap Congress placed there, this reading becomes the operative one and the encoding flips. That is why it is 'arguable' and not 'rejected'.

taken.rationale: Taken because it is the operative law. What the encoding does NOT resolve, and what this entry exists to disclose, is that the two texts differ by a factor of five on their face. 15 U.S.C. 77d(a)(6)(A) caps the exemption at $1,000,000; 17 CFR 227.100(a)(1) sets $5,000,000. Securities Act s 4A(h)(1) (15 U.S.C. 77d-1(h)(1)) requires the Commission to index the crowdfunding dollar amounts to CPI-U at least every five years, but indexation does not account for the gap: CPI-U from 2012 to 2021 takes $1,000,000 to roughly $1.15M, not to $5M. The Commission raised the cap in Release 33-10884 (2020) and the Authority note for the part claims 15 U.S.C. 77z-3. So the live question is not whether the figures differ -- they plainly do -- but whether s 28's general exemptive authority reaches a specific numeric cap Congress placed in the very paragraph being exempted. That is a question for a court, and no encoding settles it. MEASURED 2026-08-09: statutory text fetched and quoted from Cornell LII; uscode.house.gov refused the connection, so this is ONE source, not two, and the quote should be corroborated before it is relied on in print. STATUS, 2026-08-09: this entry read 'open' while carrying a `taken` reading and a `rejected` alternative, which is the encoder having taken a reading — 'resolved' under the schema's own gloss. It was 'open' because the underlying question is one for a court, but that is not what the field means: 'settled' is the value that speaks to authority, and 'resolved' says only that the encoder chose. Nothing about the reading or the disclosure changed. STATUS OF THE ALTERNATIVE, 2026-08-09: `statuteCap` moved from 'rejected' to the new 'arguable', and its rationale from `rejection_rationale` to `foreclosure`. 'rejected' means the encoder argued a reading away, and the encoder did not -- the operative text forecloses it while it remains law someone could win on. Nothing about the encoding or the disclosure changed; the register can now be queried for exposure rather than only for error.

witnesses: An issuer raising $3,000,000 in a rolling twelve months is inside the exemption under `regulationCap` and outside it under `statuteCap`. The corpus asserts the $5,000,000 figure; no fixture exercises the statutory arm, because no filer may use it.
notes: FOUND BY AUDIT, NOT BY EITHER RUN (2026-08-09). Neither the run 1 corpus nor the de novo run registered this, and the de novo run could not have: it ingested 17 CFR Part 227 from the eCFR and never fetched the instrument the part is made under. That gap is the reason P1 now requires a document with role 'instrument' (SPEC.md s 4 P1, added 2026-08-06). This entry is the first fork in either register that exists because the pipeline was made to look UP rather than forward in time.

site.anchor: `(a)(4) — a family or trust transferee, or a death-or-divorce circumstance`

source.quote: To a member of the family of the purchaser or the equivalent, to a trust controlled by the purchaser, to a trust created for the benefit of a member of the family of the purchaser or the equivalent, or in connection with the death or divorce of the purchaser or other similar circumstance.

readings.description: The closing limb asks only about the OCCASION of the transfer. A transfer made in connection with the purchaser's death or divorce, or a similar circumstance, is excepted whoever receives the securities.

The closing limb also constrains the TRANSFEREE: the recipient must be one the circumstance produces — an heir, the estate, a former spouse — so that a transfer to an unrelated stranger is outside it even if a death or a divorce occasioned it.
readings.rejection_rationale: Rejected on the escheat case. A purchaser dies intestate with no known possible heirs; the securities are sold and the proceeds escheat to the state treasury. That is squarely a transfer in connection with the death of the purchaser, and the transferee is a stranger. The nexus reading would deny the exception there, and nothing in the text supplies the recipient it would require: the first three parts of (4) name a transferee in terms ('to a ...'), and the fourth conspicuously does not.

taken.rationale: RULED 2026-08-09. The grammar decides it: the chapeau is 'unless such securities are transferred:', and limbs (1)-(3) plus the first three parts of (4) complete it as a transferee ('transferred TO x') while the last part completes it as a circumstance ('transferred IN CONNECTION WITH y'). Preserving that asymmetry is the point of decomposing the limb; flattening it into six transferee-shaped tests would be the defect the decomposition exists to repair. The encoded fields therefore keep their prepositions, and `in connection with death of the purchaser` carries the whole test on its own.

witnesses: The escheat case: a day-100 transfer with only `in connection with death of the purchaser` true, and no family member, no trust, no accredited transferee and not the issuer. `transfer is permitted` is TRUE under circumstanceAlone and FALSE under circumstanceWithNexus. Asserted in regcf.l4's Group 8a and pinned on both DMN engines as the 22nd case of jl4/examples/dmn/regcf-corpus.cases.json.
notes: Inexpressible before 2026-08-09. While limb (4) was ONE boolean field carrying all four alternatives, no fact pattern in this corpus could separate the readings: the party self-assessed the whole limb and the encoding never saw which part of it they were relying on.

site.anchor: `in connection with death of the purchaser`

source.quote: or in connection with the death or divorce of the purchaser or other similar circumstance

readings.description: Split the coordinated phrase into determiner-free fragments: `in connection with death of the purchaser`, `in connection with divorce of the purchaser`. The definite article attached to the coordination, not to each conjunct, so neither fragment inherits it.

Distribute the article across both conjuncts: `in connection with THE death of the purchaser`, `in connection with A divorce of the purchaser` (indefinite on the second, since a purchaser has one death but may have several divorces).

taken.rationale: RULED 2026-08-09: dropping invents less. Splitting a coordination forces the choice — either distribute a determiner the source never distributed, or drop it — and there is no third option that leaves the words untouched, because the words were never in the split form. Read as a test rather than as a description, the bare fragment is existential and answers the divorce question correctly: any qualifying divorce satisfies it. If a determiner is ever forced (by a renderer that cannot present a bare fragment, say), the recorded fallback is the indefinite 'a'.

notes: Divergence is 'none' on purpose, and the witnesses field is therefore absent rather than empty: the readings differ in what the field NAME says, not in what any transfer satisfies. Both are the same boolean over the same occasion, so no fact pattern separates them and none could be written.

Registered because it is a decision, not because it is a risk. The value of the entry is that a later editor who reaches for 'the death' or 'a death' can see that the bare form was chosen and why, instead of re-deciding it silently.

site.anchor: `in connection with a circumstance similar to death or divorce of the purchaser`

readings.description: 'Similar' reaches back only to 'the death or divorce of the purchaser' — the nearest coordination, and the only one it is grammatically parallel to. Its extension is circumstances of that kind: incapacity, or separation. (Those two examples are the ruling's own, recorded unnarrowed: 'separation', not 'legal separation' — the reading is not confined to a decree.)

'Similar' reaches back over the whole of limb (4), so a transfer resembling any of (4)'s transferee cases — to a household member who is not on the Rule 501(c) list, into a trust-like vehicle that is not a trust — is also within it.
readings.rejection_rationale: Rejected because it makes (4) self-swallowing: the first three parts would become examples rather than requirements, and the Rule 501(c) definition of 'member of the family of the purchaser or the equivalent' — which the Commission wrote a whole paragraph to fix — could be routed around by asserting similarity to it. A catch-all at the end of a list does not ordinarily reopen the list's own defined terms.

taken.rationale: RULED 2026-08-09. The field name says which reading was taken, in the name itself: `in connection with a circumstance similar to death or divorce of the purchaser`, not `similar circumstance`. That is a deliberate departure from the source's wording — the source says only 'or other similar circumstance' — and it is made because the shorter form would carry the ambiguity into the question a lay holder is asked. What the encoding cannot do is decide the boundary: 'similar' remains vague, and the field asks the party to place their own facts inside or outside it.

witnesses: A transfer to a long-term housemate who is not a Rule 501(c) relation — a cohabitant, but not one 'occupying a relationship generally equivalent to that of a spouse', which is where 501(c)'s spousal-equivalent limb stops — made for no reason connected with a death or a divorce, is outside the limb under similarToDeathOrDivorce and arguably inside it under similarToAllOfLimb4. The corpus refuses it: the six fields have no arm the facts fit.
notes: The decomposition STOPS at 'member of the family of the purchaser or the equivalent'. 17 CFR 227.501(c) defines that term with 'includes' over FOURTEEN enumerated relationships, and 'shall include adoptive relationships' on top, so it is an OPEN list; enumerating it as fourteen booleans would encode an open term as a closed one, which is a larger fidelity loss than the one the decomposition repairs. It stays one boolean deliberately, and that is the reason. COUNTING METHOD, because the number was wrong once already: fourteen comma-separated slots in the definition — child, stepchild, grandchild, parent, stepparent, grandparent, 'spouse or spousal equivalent' (one slot, not two), sibling, and the six in-laws (mother-, father-, son-, daughter-, brother-, sister-). Splitting spouse from spousal equivalent gives fifteen; no counting gives thirteen. Four sibling texts carried that figure and were corrected on 2026-08-09: regcf.l4's decomposition comment, regcf-wizard.l4's family-limb explanation, the s2-07 narrative, and — deliberately NOT corrected — denovo/regcf-denovo.l4:1277, which is the independent G2 encoding and is not ours to edit.

Vagueness, not competing parses: unlike F-501A4-NEXUS there is no second grammar here that a court would have to choose between, only a term whose extension is not fixed. Registered under kind 'vagueness' for that reason.
